headline: Seventy Eight Plays, Fifty Five Cents Lost, Zero Stories Told
paragraphs: Sixty seven games got graded, twenty two were deemed unworthy of an opinion, and forty five produced seventy eight tickets at ten dollars each. Seven hundred eighty dollars went out the door and seven hundred seventy nine dollars and forty five cents came back. That is a loss of fifty five cents, an ROI of negative one tenth of one percent, and the single most elaborate way imaginable to accomplish absolutely nothing. The model expected to hit 61.8 percent. It hit 52.0.

The one that worked was Tulsa and Florida Atlantic, Under 73, a ten point eight point edge that landed on 38-21 without ever breathing hard. The one that did not was Colorado State at Washington State, where the model bought the moneyline at plus 300 with a 14.9 probability point edge, took the points at plus 8.5, and played Under 65 for good measure. Final score 73-7. Three tickets, three losses, one genuinely impressive display of commitment to a bad idea. The published top five went 2-3 for a loss of eleven dollars and eighty two cents, which is to say the five picks we actually asked readers to look at lost twenty three point six percent while the other seventy three roughly broke even.

By market, spreads made three dollars and sixty two cents, totals made ninety cents, and moneylines gave back five dollars and seven cents, a distribution so flat it barely qualifies as information. Sixty three lines moved and only nineteen of them, 30.2 percent, moved our way, which is the market politely declining to agree. Season sits at 226-279-15 across 520 plays and eight real graded weeks, down five hundred eighty six dollars and fifty nine cents at negative 11.3 percent ROI. Breaking even this week was, by recent standards, a triumph.
